summary: PRECIS defines classes of strings for use in application protocols. Since many protocols compare strings with or without regard to case, this informational RFC defines methods for case mapping. It also defines other mappings such as for width and for special characters.

eli5.summary: Computers need to decide when two spellings count as the same, like capital and small letters. This gives the rules for treating them equally.

questions: what is precis local case mapping
subtitle: Extra character mappings that make internationalized strings compare the way users expect.

tldr.problem: The PRECIS framework maps case and width, but users also type look-alike delimiters, odd spaces and letters whose lowercase form depends on language.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines delimiter mapping, special mapping and local case mapping as protocol-dependent extras, and recommends applying delimiter mapping before special mapping.
tldr.outcome: Profile designers get guidelines and examples. The RFC is Informational and inherits the security considerations of the PRECIS framework.

today: RFC 7790 is an Informational IETF document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It supplements the PRECIS framework in RFC 7564.

sections.title: Why More Mappings Are Needed
sections.content:
Users often enter internationalized strings through an input method editor (IME) or by copy and paste. They usually do not care about the case or width of characters, because the results look equivalent, and they rarely switch the IME state to type special characters such as protocol elements.

The PRECIS framework (RFC 7564) defines case mapping and width mapping. It does not handle delimiters, special characters, or locale-dependent and context-dependent case. This document gives guidelines for authors of PRECIS profiles. Delimiter mapping and special mapping are applied as additional mappings, while local case mapping is an alternative case mapping for specific characters. For domain names, the IDNA mapping document is RFC 5895.
sections.eli5: People type text in lots of ways that look the same to them but not to a computer. These rules close that gap.

sections.title: Delimiter Mapping and Special Mapping
sections.content:
Both mappings depend on the rules of a particular application protocol, so each protocol should base its table on a well-defined mapping.

Delimiter mapping turns characters that resemble a protocol delimiter into the real delimiter. Examples are width-compatible forms of @ in email addresses and of : and / in URIs. Another is the IDEOGRAPHIC FULL STOP (U+3002), which some IMEs produce when the user types FULL STOP (U+002E).

Special mapping covers other protocol-specific changes. White space such as CHARACTER TABULATION (U+0009) or IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE (U+3000) is mapped to SPACE (U+0020), and some characters such as control characters are mapped to nothing. The RFC says EAP, the IMAP4 ACL extension and LDAPprep define rules that map some non-ASCII spaces to SPACE.
sections.eli5: Delimiter mapping swaps look-alike punctuation for the real one. Special mapping turns odd spaces into plain spaces and drops invisible junk.

sections.title: Local Case Mapping
sections.content:
Local case mapping aims to give the result users expect when case changes between input and use in a protocol. It applies only to characters whose case mapping depends on locale or context. The usual example is LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I (U+0049), which normally becomes LATIN SMALL LETTER I (U+0069), but in Turkish and some other languages becomes LATIN SMALL LETTER DOTLESS I (U+0131), unless the I is before a dot above.

The possible target characters are those in SpecialCasing.txt of the Unicode Standard. A selected target character is mapped to lowercase as defined there. All other characters use the case folding in section 5.2.3 of the PRECIS framework.

Local case mapping and Unicode Default Case Folding are alternatives and cannot be applied together or one after the other. Appendix B explains one reason to choose it: default folding turns the German eszett (U+00DF) into two s characters, while the SpecialCasing mapping keeps it as one code point. Appendix C notes a limit. Unicode (up to version 7.0.0) defines no context-dependent mapping between small sigma and final sigma, so the PRECIS framework always maps final sigma to small sigma.
sections.eli5: Some letters change case differently depending on the language, like the letter I in Turkish. Local case mapping lets an app follow the user's language when it changes capitals to small letters.

sections.title: Order of Operations
sections.content: Delimiter mapping and special mapping are expected to be applied as the Additional Mapping Rule from section 5.2.2 of the PRECIS framework. They could be applied in either order, but the RFC recommends doing delimiter mapping first and special mapping second. The goal is to limit the effect of code-point changes and to suit the widest user community.
sections.eli5: First swap look-alike punctuation, then clean up the spaces. Doing it in that order causes the fewest surprises.

sections.title: Mappings in Older Protocols
sections.content:
Appendix A lists which kinds of mapping earlier protocols used. These are protocols built on the stringprep framework (RFC 3454), which the RFC treats as candidates for PRECIS, since stringprep and the related IDNA versions in the table are now obsolete.

The table covers IDNA (RFC 3490 and RFC 3491), iSCSI (RFC 3722), EAP (RFC 3748), IMAP ACL (RFC 4314) and LDAP (RFC 4518). Each uses a different mix of width, delimiter, case and special mapping.
sections.eli5: Older internet systems each picked their own mix of these clean-up steps. A chart shows who used which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document inherits the security considerations of the PRECIS framework (RFC 7564). Like the IDNA mapping document (RFC 5895), it suggests mappings that may confuse some users while reducing confusion for others. The RFC says this confusion is not covered in any depth.
sections.eli5: Tidying text can help some people and puzzle others. The RFC points to another document for the full safety discussion.
